Damian Paletta
 
Howard Lutnick Needs Friends After Spending Two Years Making Enemies
 
Plus, Trump tells Vance to focus on domestic issues, and U.S. Army officer identified after arrest in U.K. for alleged Russian spying
 
 
LEV RADIN/ZUMA PRESS
 

Good morning. Less than 12 hours after Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia’s CEO, congressional Democrats spun their scrutiny to a high-profile member of the Trump administration: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

 

Top Democrats on two key congressional panels sent Lutnick a letter saying they had started an investigation into the Trump administration’s export plans as they relate to Nvidia. 

 

This might sound like pretty wonky stuff, but it’s a multibillion-dollar mess that involves national security, trade policy, and—according to Democrats—an opening for wrongdoing and corruption.

 

Just a couple of days ago, lawmakers were focused on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth gave a full-throated defense of himself in a press conference (which elated President Trump), and he survived an impeachment attempt.

 

Can Lutnick similarly circle wagons?

 

Democrats aren’t angling to impeach Lutnick necessarily, but the White House can’t afford the ugly Nvidia news cycle to drag on much longer. Lutnick and Trump have known each other for years, but Lutnick’s brash bravado has unsettled a number of other top officials. (He and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have had some famous tangles, for example). 

 

If Lutnick is on the political ropes, will people rush in to save him? Or could he follow Huang out of his job because the company’s newly scrutinized ties to the U.S. government open up uncomfortable questions about the Commerce Department?

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Meredith O’Rourke: Congressional Democrats have opened an investigation into Trump’s top fundraiser.

 

Sen. Chris Van Hollen: The Democratic senator from Maryland said he would challenge current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.) to lead Senate Democrats in the majority next year.

 

Trump’s Friday: The president has policy meetings throughout the day.

What I’m Following

 
 
KEVIN LAMARQUE/REUTERS
 

Trump told the vice president to focus on domestic crime instead of Iran. In a social-media post, the president said Vice President JD Vance should focus his efforts on crime and corruption in the U.S., rather than striking a peace deal with Iran. Trump said that such an agreement wasn’t necessary, a move that comes as Vance had opened a channel with Iran’s hard-line security chief and was positioning himself as Washington’s top negotiator.

 

The U.S. Army officer arrested after a U.K. sting for alleged Russian spying has been identified. Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner was assigned to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at the time of his arrest near Gloucester in the U.K. He had joined the Army in 2008 and had previously served in Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq. U.S. officials say he unwittingly spoke with British authorities, and his motive still isn’t clear.

 

The U.S. cut Cuba off from the world’s oil, and now the island runs on American fuel. The Trump administration’s oil embargo on Cuba has produced an unlikely result: The U.S. is now its primary fuel supplier. The administration began allowing U.S. fuel sales to private businesses on the island just weeks after the embargo began, and since then, U.S. ports have shipped more than 1.6 million barrels of fuel, worth over $230 million.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• One person was killed and four were wounded in a Washington, D.C. shooting.

 

• Ukraine said it’s American military-grade Starlink satellite internet service, known as Starshield, was disrupted again, hurting its defenses.

 

• As the U.S. war with Iran grinds on, Tehran is flexing a new level of aggression that cybersecurity experts warn make it a more dangerous foe.

 

• Former President Joe Biden’s scaled-back book tour rekindles questions over his health.
